sentences.text: This is part two of Powers, Logarithms and Oscillations, on De Moivre's theorem.
Last time, you solved zed to the fifth equals two eye, and found five roots, spaced evenly round a ring.
The key was that multiplying complex numbers adds their angles, so a fifth power multiplies an angle by five.
Today's question sounds like plain trigonometry.
What is cosine of four theta, written using only cosine theta?
You could use the double-angle formula twice, since four is two times two.
But for cosine of seven theta, you'd be stacking compound-angle formulas, line after line.
De Moivre's theorem gets any of them from a single power.
Start with a complex number of modulus one, at angle theta.
It's cosine theta, plus eye sine theta, and by Euler's formula, that's E to the eye theta.
Now raise it to a whole-number power, N.
Here, as in the notes, N is the power.
It's no longer the count of full turns from last time.
When you raise an exponential to a power, you multiply the exponents.
So E to the eye theta, to the power N, is E to the eye N theta.
And by Euler's formula again, that's cosine of N theta, plus eye sine of N theta.
Set the first expression equal to the last, and you have De Moivre's theorem.
Cosine of N theta, plus eye sine of N theta, equals cosine theta plus eye sine theta, all to the power N.
Here's what that means in the plane.
Multiplying complex numbers multiplies their lengths and adds their angles.
So the arrow times itself points at angle two theta.
Times itself again, three theta.

Each step turns it by another theta, and its length stays one, because one times one is still one.

Let's recap.
De Moivre's theorem says that E to the eye theta, to the power N, is E to the eye N theta, the arrow turned to angle N theta.
The power N must be a whole number, because a fraction splits the full turns into several values.
To expand a power, use Pascal's row, and let the powers of eye sort the real terms from the imaginary ones.
Matching real parts, then imaginary parts, gives cosine and sine of four theta.
And adding or subtracting two mirror-image arrows writes cosine and sine as exponentials.
